name: Proverbs
v: Son, hold tight to what I say. Store my commands deep inside you.
Guard them and live. Treat my teaching like the pupil of your eye.
Tie them around your fingers. Carve them onto the walls of your heart.
Tell wisdom, "You're my sister." Call understanding your closest friend.
They'll keep you clear of the seductress — the smooth-talking stranger who knows exactly what she's doing.
One day I stood at my window, peering through the lattice,
and I watched the street. Among the clueless, the easily-led, I spotted a young man with no sense at all.
He took the corner near her house — strolling, casual — and headed straight down her street.
Twilight was falling. Evening dimmed into night, and the dark closed in.
And there she came to meet him — dressed like a prostitute, calculating behind her eyes.
Loud. Restless. The kind of woman whose feet refuse to stay home —
always out in the street, in the squares, lurking on every corner.
She grabbed him. Kissed him. Looked him dead in the face and said, without a flicker of shame:
"I owed a peace offering today, and I paid my vows.
So I came looking for you — wanted you specifically — and here you are.
I've made the bed up with colored linens, fine Egyptian fabric.
I've drenched the sheets in myrrh, aloes, cinnamon.
Come on. Let's drink love till morning. Let's lose ourselves in each other.
My husband isn't home. He's gone — far away.
Took the money bag with him. Won't be back till the full moon."
She wore him down with her words. Her smooth lips reeled him in.
He followed her like an ox walking to slaughter — like a deer stepping into the snare,
until an arrow goes through its liver. Like a bird flying straight into the net, never seeing it was about to die.
So listen to me, sons. Pay attention. Hear what I'm telling you.
Don't let your heart wander her direction. Don't drift onto her streets.
She has dropped countless men. Her body count is staggering.
Her house is a highway to the grave, descending straight to the chambers of death.

com.d:
# Proverbs 7: The Power of Wisdom Against Seduction

Proverbs 7 offers a sobering call to spiritual vigilance, showing us that wisdom isn't abstract knowledge but a living defense against the forces that would draw us away from God's design for our lives. Through the vivid narrative of a young man seduced by an adulteress, Solomon teaches us that our greatest vulnerabilities often come when we wander from the boundaries God has established.

The passage opens with a tender invitation: "Keep my words as the apple of your eye." Solomon speaks as a father who loves his son, wanting him to hold wisdom close and precious, like something irreplaceable. This isn't stern obligation but passionate protection. Then he shows why we need it—by narrating the slow, methodical seduction of a naive young man who lacks understanding. The adulteress doesn't attack directly; she uses flattery, timing, sensuality, and the promise of forbidden pleasure. She catches him at dusk when judgment grows cloudy and isolation makes him vulnerable. Notice how the passage emphasizes his lack of sense; he "follows her as an ox to the slaughter."

What makes this passage pierce our hearts is its honesty about temptation's power. It rarely announces itself with evil fanfare. Instead, it whispers, it flatters, it promises freedom while weaving chains. Whether the temptation is sexual, financial, relational, or spiritual, it typically works through gradual steps away from wisdom's guardrails. The young man didn't plan to be destroyed; he simply neglected to stay close to wisdom and didn't guard the boundaries that would have protected him.

Solomon's remedy remains unchanged: keep wisdom close, treasure God's Word, meditate on it, let it shape your steps. Wisdom isn't a wet blanket but a loving guide who keeps us from paths that lead to loss. She calls to us from the streets, inviting us toward life, safety, and wholeness.

Where might you be drifting from the protective boundaries wisdom has established in your life? What would it look like to draw closer to God's Word this week?
com.s:
Proverbs 7 constitutes one of the most vivid and dramatically crafted warnings in the wisdom literature of ancient Israel, continuing the extended discourse on sexual fidelity that dominates chapters 5–7 of this collection. The chapter is attributed to Solomon, though the final compilation of Proverbs likely occurred during the reign of Hezekiah, as indicated in 25:1. This particular instruction takes the form of a father's urgent appeal to his son, reflecting the pedagogical setting of the ancient Israelite household where wisdom was transmitted intergenerationally through careful mentorship and memorable illustration.

The passage opens with the familiar imperative to guard the father's commandments, employing the Hebrew term *mitswah* (מִצְוָה), which carries covenantal overtones linking parental instruction to divine Torah. The exhortation to bind these teachings on one's fingers and write them on the tablet of the heart echoes Deuteronomy 6:8–9, suggesting that wisdom instruction participates in the same authoritative sphere as revealed law. The sage further instructs the youth to call wisdom "sister" (*'achot*, אָחוֹת), utilizing kinship language that establishes an intimate, protective relationship with personified wisdom as a counter to the seductive stranger.

The narrative core of the chapter presents a firsthand account, ostensibly observed through a window, of a young man lacking sense (*chasar-lev*, חֲסַר־לֵב) who succumbs to the elaborate enticements of the "strange woman" (*'ishah zarah*). Her characterization draws on imagery of cultic prostitution, foreign religious practices, and covenant unfaithfulness, though scholars debate whether the figure represents literal adultery, apostasy from Yahweh worship, or a wisdom-theological construct opposing Lady Wisdom of chapters 1 and 8. Her lips drip with honey and her speech is smoother than oil, inverting the positive attributes elsewhere assigned to wisdom herself.

The dramatic movement toward destruction employs powerful similes—an ox to slaughter, a deer stepping into a snare—culminating in the solemn declaration that her house is the way to Sheol. Within the canonical structure, this chapter prepares for the magnificent celebration of personified Wisdom in chapter 8, establishing through negative example the life-and-death stakes that wisdom's call represents for the covenant community.
com.p:
Proverbs 7 emerges from the golden age of Israel's united monarchy, penned approximately one thousand years before Christ's advent, during the reign of Solomon when Israel stood at the zenith of its wisdom tradition. This places the passage firmly within the Kingdom era of redemptive history, after God had established David's throne and promised an eternal dynasty, yet before the tragic division and eventual exile that would scatter God's people. Solomon, himself a type of the greater Wisdom who would come, here transmits divine instruction that transcends his own moral failures and points toward ultimate realities.

The chapter unfolds as a father's urgent warning against the adulterous woman who prowls the streets at twilight, seducing the simple youth toward destruction. Yet this is far more than domestic counsel about sexual purity. Throughout Scripture, adultery functions as the primary metaphor for Israel's spiritual infidelity—her recurring temptation to forsake Yahweh, her true Husband, for the seductive gods of the nations. The woman dressed as a harlot, with her smooth words and perfumed bed, embodies the same ancient serpentine voice that whispered in Eden, promising pleasure while concealing death. Her house leads down to Sheol; her chambers are the very paths to death. Here stands the antitype of Lady Wisdom from chapters one through nine, representing the cosmic choice set before every human soul.

The prophetic dimension deepens when we recognize that Christ Himself is the true Wisdom calling in the streets, the faithful Bridegroom who never deceives. Where the adulterous woman leads her lovers to slaughter like an ox, Christ the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep. The simple youth, ensnared through weakness and wandering, pictures all humanity in Adam—easily deceived, drawn toward forbidden fruit, walking ignorantly toward judgment. Yet the cross reveals a Bridegroom who pursued His wayward bride not to destroy her but to redeem her through His own blood.

The church age finds believers betrothed to Christ, awaiting the marriage supper of the Lamb. The seductive voices of the present age—false teaching, worldly enticement, spiritual compromise—still call from darkened streets. This proverb therefore remains urgently prophetic, warning the covenant community to guard their hearts, bind wisdom's words upon their fingers, and recognize that faithfulness to Christ requires the same vigilant love that marriage demands. The path of wisdom leads to life eternal; the way of folly ends in everlasting death.
